attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: Present-tense factual claim that the apparent demand is almost entirely debt-funded. The normalised wording keeps the scare quotes' sense ('apparent demand') and the 'almost entirely' quantifier.

contract.note: In context, 'that demand' is the demand cited from NVIDIA/Samsung guidance, which mostly comes from hyperscalers. Reading 'almost entirely' as roughly 80-90% or more is ordinary. A narrower reading (only private-credit data center deals) is possible but is not the plain one.

evidence.note: Alphabet Q1 2026 filing: operating cash flow of $45.8B exceeded $35.7B capex. A top AI compute buyer's buildout was covered by operating cash.
Meta Q1 2026: operating cash flow of $32.2B and positive free cash flow after $19.8B capex. The buildout was funded from operations.
Alphabet raised $31.1B in notes in Q1 2026, so debt was significant. But operating cash alone covered capex, so debt was not almost the whole source.

reviews.rationale: Two of the largest AI compute buyers (Alphabet, Meta) paid for their Q1 2026 capex out of operating cash flow, with cash left over. That meets the contract's contradiction condition. Heavy debt issuance and the debt reliance of neoclouds and developers are real but unquantified. They cannot make debt 'almost entirely' the funding source when major hyperscaler spending was cash-funded.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Categorical present-state claim ('aren't happening at all') about profitability and ROI for the AI businesses of the named executives. The 'tangible proof' part is rhetorical.

contract.note: Reading 'aren't happening at all' as no actual profit from AI-driven businesses is an ordinary reading of categorical language. Counting infrastructure profit (cloud, NVIDIA) is debatable but not stretched: Google Cloud is run by one of the named executives, and the company links its growth to AI.

evidence.note: Alphabet says Google Cloud's 63% growth was led by enterprise AI solutions and infrastructure. This links the segment's profit to AI. It is a company disclosure.
Google Cloud segment operating income was $6.6B in Q1 2026, up from $2.2B. That is reported profit from an AI-driven unit under Pichai.

NVIDIA, whose revenue is mostly data center sales, reported strong GAAP earnings for the quarter ended April 2026. That is AI-industry profitability, though NVIDIA is not among the named executives' firms.

reviews.rationale: The claim says profitability 'isn't happening at all'. In the target period, Google Cloud (Pichai) reported sharply higher operating income that Alphabet attributes mainly to AI demand, and NVIDIA reported large AI-driven profits. Returns on hyperscaler AI capex and AI-lab profitability are not separately shown. But the categorical profitability claim fails on the plain reading.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Two linked causal claims: VC money is the only reason Perplexity and Lovable survive, and therefore a large chunk of both Anthropic's and OpenAI's API revenue depends on it. The normalised wording keeps both parts.

contract.note: Requiring both parts, for both labs, is faithful to 'both'. A large-chunk threshold of about a fifth to a quarter is a reasonable plain reading. The counterfactual cannot be observed directly.

evidence.note: Secondary report (Sept 2026) says much of Anthropic's recent growth came from its own products and enterprises. It gives no VC-dependent share of API revenue and nothing on OpenAI.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no profit or cash-flow data for Perplexity or Lovable. It also has no breakdown of either lab's API revenue by customer funding source. The one item is suggestive context about Anthropic only. The evidence does not settle either part of the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps the $1T and 30GW model claims and the 'appears' hedge. The checkable core is the present-state ceiling: '5GW at most' under construction. 'Appears' softens it, but the explicit ceiling makes it a firm factual assertion, not a probability.

contract.note: Set against 30GW needed by 2028, '5GW under construction' ordinarily means total capacity under construction. Leaving the $1T and 30GW model assumptions unscored is fair. Even the narrow 2026-scheduled reading is contradicted by Jefferies.

evidence.note: June 2026 Jefferies note via The Register: about 12GW of US capacity scheduled for 2026 was under construction. That is more than double the ceiling, even within the narrow subset.
CBRE (published Aug 2026, covering H1 2026): 7,481MW under construction in eight primary North American markets alone. That is above 5GW.
BNEF: 23.1GW under construction globally at end-September 2025. This is before the target period, but it shows the totals were far above 5GW.
Sightline/Currence (April 2026): about 5GW under construction among 2026-slated projects over 50MW. This is the likely source and supports only a narrow reading.

reviews.rationale: Independent trackers for H1 2026 report materially more than 5GW under construction: about 12GW of US 2026-scheduled capacity (Jefferies) and about 7.5GW in just eight primary North American markets (CBRE). The 5GW figure matches one tracker's narrow subset. It does not hold as a ceiling on capacity under construction. The $1T and 30GW parts are model assumptions and are not scored.
